Foundations · Chapter 01 of 28

01 Purpose

Learn what Oath & Action does, and how its pillars and nonpartisan rules shape every piece.

Oath & Action is a nonpartisan publication and a set of tools for people in every state who live under public rules they rarely get to read. Our mission is “Help people understand and improve the rules that shape their lives.”

The ampersand in our name is the hinge, the joint a door swings on. It joins a promise to the action that keeps it, so every piece explains and tracks a decision, then turns to the people who make it and the step a reader can take. Chapter 04 draws the hinge and sets its rules.

Rules in this chapter, by group

  1. 1 Color and party
    • 01.1 Keep red off every party, side and person.
    • 01.2 Draw every party in one neutral ink, with its name on the mark.
    • 01.3 Run a two-way scale from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris.
    • 01.4 On Prussian, turn identity marks White and data marks Newsprint.
    • 01.5 Color a map by the rule or measure the story covers.
  2. 2 Pictures
    • 01.6 Show domes, columns and flags only in a captioned photograph of that place.
    • 01.7 Keep party symbols, candidate photos, campaign gear and protest slogans out of brand graphics.
    • 01.8 Photograph people doing public work, and caption who, what, where and when.
  3. 3 Choosing examples
    • 01.9 Draw no more than one example in four from one atlas domain, or one in five from one state.
    • 01.10 Rotate examples across levels of government and regions.
    • 01.11 When majorities of both parties use a mechanism, show a case from each.
    • 01.12 Log each example’s domain, state, region, level and backing coalition.
  4. 4 Words
    • 01.13 Name the office that decides, and name a party only when party is the mechanism.
    • 01.14 Ask questions a supporter of the current rule could ask too.
    • 01.15 Use plain verbs in place of war and sports metaphors.
    • 01.16 Show both readings of a contested claim at the same length.
    • 01.17 Describe a rule so its supporters would accept the description.
  5. 5 Hinge headlines
    • 01.18 Set both halves of a hinge headline in one color and weight, and give the red to the ampersand.
    • 01.19 Join people through a rule or place they share, and rotate their order.
    • 01.20 Name parties, the left or the right in a hinge headline only to report sourced agreement.
  6. 6 Labels, Act pieces and names
    • 01.21 Open every kicker with one content label.
    • 01.22 In a process piece, name the step and leave the side to the reader.
    • 01.23 Put a position piece’s label before the headline and its fairness kit before the ask.
    • 01.24 Name each product for what it does, and keep the ampersand for Oath & Action.

Group 1 Color and party

Give no party, side or person a color of its own, and print every name on its mark.

Rule 01.1 Keep red off every party, side and person.

Pillar Red never stands for a party, one side of a debate or a named person, in a chart, a map, a label or a headline. Each view gives its one working red to the job Rule 05.3 names, and none of those jobs is a side.

Tokens

  • --oa-chart-color-party-mark-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Election-night maps have taught readers to see red as one party. A red mark on a side tells a reader on the other side that the piece is against them before they read a word, and they stop trusting the record we keep for everyone.

Specifications

Working red
One job per view, in the order Rule 05.3 sets
--oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint
Sides of a vote
One neutral ink, names and counts printed
--oa-chart-color-party-mark-on-newsprint

Related chapters

  • 05 Color
  • 14 Data visualization Coming later

For builders

Search the piece for Pillar Red and name each red mark’s job. If a mark stands for a party, a side or a person, redraw it in the party mark ink with its name printed.

Rule 01.2 Draw every party in one neutral ink, with its name on the mark.

When a chart, map or table shows parties, draw every party’s mark in the same neutral ink, Charcoal on Newsprint, and print the party’s name on or beside its mark. Where two sides must be told apart at a glance, draw one solid and one in outline, in that same ink. Red never stands against blue or Verdigris.

Tokens

  • --oa-chart-color-party-mark-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Red against blue reads as an election before it reads as data, and red against Verdigris stages the same contest in other hues. One ink gives every party the same weight, and a printed name lets a reader see who is who without learning a color code, in color or in grayscale.

Specifications

Party marks
Charcoal, one ink for every party
--oa-chart-color-party-mark-on-newsprint
Two sides at a glance
One solid and one in outline, in the same ink
Names
Printed on or beside each mark, in the text ink
Order
Alphabetical, unless the data sets another order

Related chapters

  • 05 Color
  • 14 Data visualization Coming later

For builders

Use the party mark token for every party, never a palette color by name, and set each party’s name as a direct label.

Rule 01.3 Run a two-way scale from Prussian through the page color to Verdigris.

A scale that shows change in two directions runs from Prussian through Newsprint to Verdigris. A boxed arrow and a word name each step’s direction, because the two hues lose their order in grayscale. Red and blue never form a two-way pair.

Tokens

  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step1-on-newsprint#1F2D5A
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step2-on-newsprint#8E94A4
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step3-on-newsprint#CECDC7
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step4-on-newsprint#9AAEA6
  • --oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step5-on-newsprint#3C5F59

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Neither end of the pair belongs to a party, so a fall and a rise carry the same weight. The arrow and the word carry the direction for a reader who sees no color at all.

Specifications

Steps
Five, step 1 the strongest fall, step 3 the page color
--oa-chart-color-diverging-fill-step3-on-newsprint
Direction
A boxed arrow in each step’s label ink, and a word

Rule 01.4 On Prussian, turn identity marks White and data marks Newsprint.

On a Prussian ground, set every identity mark in one color, White, the ampersand included. Draw data graphics on Prussian in Newsprint. Red never sits on Prussian.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-prussian#FFFFFF
  • --oa-color-data-emphasis-on-prussian#DCD9D2

Why it works

Basis Design judgment, measured against WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 at rendered sizes

Pillar Red measures 3.19 to 1 against Prussian, which passes the 3 to 1 WCAG asks of marks until the size drops. At 16 px, where smoothing thins the strokes, the red ampersand measures 2.27 to 1 and a White one 8.27 to 1. Red on our dark blue also pairs the two colors election maps give the parties.

Specifications

Identity marks
White, one color
--oa-color-identity-signature-on-prussian
Data marks
Newsprint
--oa-color-data-emphasis-on-prussian

Rule 01.5 Color a map by the rule or measure the story covers.

Color a map by the rule, count or measure the story is about, never by which party won each place. Use the neutral palette or a pattern, and set the key beside the map.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-data-emphasis-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-border-strong-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A map colored by winner splits the country into two camps and gives large, thinly settled states the most ink. What a reader wants to know is whether a rule reaches the place where they live.

Specifications

Tile grid
12 columns by 8 rows, one square per state and DC
Fills
Charcoal, a Charcoal hatch and open, keyed in words
--oa-color-data-emphasis-on-newsprint

Group 2 Pictures

Show real places and people doing public work, with a caption a reader can check.

Rule 01.6 Show domes, columns and flags only in a captioned photograph of that place.

Show a capitol dome, columns or a flag only inside a documentary photograph of that place or event, with a caption that names it. Keep them out of icons, backgrounds and textures.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Campaigns in both parties use the dome and the flag as shorthand for government. As decoration they stand for no rule, office or event, so they give the reader nothing to check or act on.

Related chapters

  • 16 Photography, illustration and video Coming later
  • 12 Graphic devices and patterns Coming later

For builders

Build cards from type and the brand’s own devices. A dome, a column or a flag enters only with a documentary photograph, its caption and its credit.

Rule 01.7 Keep party symbols, candidate photos, campaign gear and protest slogans out of brand graphics.

Keep party symbols, candidate photographs, campaign merchandise and legible protest slogans out of brand graphics, since each takes a side the piece never argued. A party’s logo may appear as evidence, inside a sourced document the piece reproduces.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader takes any symbol on our page as ours. A campaign button or a slogan placard reads as an endorsement, even when the story beside it is neutral.

Related chapters

  • 16 Photography, illustration and video Coming later
  • 23 Social and video Coming later

For builders

When a story needs a party’s logo or a campaign’s material, place the whole document as a sourced image with its credit, never the symbol by itself.

Rule 01.8 Photograph people doing public work, and caption who, what, where and when.

Choose photographs of people of different ages, places and roles doing public work, officials among them. Every caption names who is shown, what they are doing, where and when.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader trusts a picture of a real hearing more than a picture of the idea of one, and a full caption lets them check it.

Related chapters

  • 16 Photography, illustration and video Coming later

For builders

Write the caption’s four parts before a photograph goes in: who, what, where and when.

Group 3 Choosing examples

Spread examples across subjects, states, regions and levels of government, and log each one so anyone can count them.

Rule 01.9 Draw no more than one example in four from one atlas domain, or one in five from one state.

Count examples within one unit: a chapter of this guide, a report, or a month of newsletter issues. Draw no more than one in four from any one of our systems atlas’s ten domains, and no more than one in five from any one state.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A run of examples from one subject or one state tells readers whose problems we care about. Rotation keeps a reader in Texas and a reader in Maine in view of the same chapter.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later

For builders

Count from the rotation log before a chapter, report or month of issues runs, using the atlas’s ten domains by their full names.

Rule 01.10 Rotate examples across levels of government and regions.

Draw examples from federal, state, county or city, and school district decisions, and from every region of the country: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South and the West.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Most of the rules that reach a household are written below the federal level. A reader who only ever sees Congress learns that the decisions nearest to them are not worth following.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later
  • 21 The atlas Coming later

For builders

Tag each row of the rotation log with its level and region, and look for an empty one before the piece runs.

Rule 01.11 When majorities of both parties use a mechanism, show a case from each.

When majorities of both parties use the same mechanism, show a documented case from each, described in the same form and at the same length. The test case is Loop R4a, the map-drawing loop, which our systems atlas titles “Majorities draw maps that help them keep control.”

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A mechanism shown through one party’s case reads as a charge against that party. With a case from each side, told the same way, the mechanism itself stands out, and that is the part a reader can change.

Related chapters

  • 15 Systems graphics Coming later
  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later

For builders

Before a piece runs a mechanism, list the party of the majority in each of the atlas’s case records for that loop, pick one case from each and write both in the same form.

Rule 01.12 Log each example’s domain, state, region, level and backing coalition.

Log every example with its atlas domain, its state and region, its level of government and, for any reform shown, the coalition that usually backs it. Our editors review the log before each chapter, report or series runs.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A chapter can lean toward one topic or one side without anyone noticing. A log turns balance into counts anyone can check, including a reader who suspects a lean.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later
  • 28 Standards checklist Coming later

For builders

Keep one log row per example in the piece’s notes and count domains, states and regions from it before it runs.

Group 4 Words

Name the office that decides, and describe every rule in words its supporters would accept.

Rule 01.13 Name the office that decides, and name a party only when party is the mechanism.

Say which office or body makes the decision. Name a party only when party is part of how the decision works, such as a party-line vote, and give the count and its source.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader can call an office or testify before it, and at the next election they can vote out its members or the official who appointed them. A party’s name in place of an office gives them a team to blame and nobody to call.

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice
  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later

For builders

Search a draft for “politicians”, “Washington”, “lawmakers” and party names, and replace each with the office that holds the decision.

Rule 01.14 Ask questions a supporter of the current rule could ask too.

Leave grievance words out of headlines, questions and calls to act, such as “rigged”, “broken”, “crisis” and “the rule you are angry about”. Write each question so a person who supports the current rule could ask it too.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A question that assumes the reader is angry tells half our readers the piece is for someone else. Who decided, and when the rule could change, are things a reader on either side of it wants to know.

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice
  • 23 Social and video Coming later

For builders

Search a draft for the words this rule lists, and read each question as someone who likes the current rule would.

Rule 01.15 Use plain verbs in place of war and sports metaphors.

Describe a public decision in the words for what happens, such as propose, debate, vote and pass. Leave out war and sports metaphors such as fight, battle, front and game plan.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A war or a game needs an enemy or a loser, and the people on the other side of a vote are our readers too. The verbs for what happens also tell a reader where the decision stands.

Related chapters

  • 02 Voice

For builders

Search a draft for fight, battle, front, war and game plan, and name the step in the process in its place.

Rule 01.16 Show both readings of a contested claim at the same length.

When credible studies disagree, give the two readings equal length, the same verbs and the same type, and name who holds each one in the same form.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Equal space is how a reader sees that the disagreement is real. A long reading beside a short dismissal, or a credential on one side and a tag on the other, tells them which side we prefer before they weigh either.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later
  • 14 Data visualization Coming later

For builders

Set both readings in one two-column block with matching labels, describe both holders in the same words, and count the words of each before you publish.

Rule 01.17 Describe a rule so its supporters would accept the description.

Read your description of a rule as someone who supports it would. If they would object to the words, rewrite the description until they would accept it, and save the argument for a labeled position piece.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Readers who back a rule are among the people we serve, and many are the officials we ask readers to contact, so the description has to hold for them as well.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later
  • 02 Voice

For builders

Before review, read the description in the place of someone who supports the rule, and mark every word they would change.

Group 5 Hinge headlines

Keep both halves equal and join people only through something they share; Rule 02.27 sets how to write a hinge headline and Rule 04.3 how to draw one.

Rule 01.18 Set both halves of a hinge headline in one color and weight, and give the red to the ampersand.

Set both noun phrases of a hinge headline in the same ink, face and weight. The ampersand takes the view’s working red, unless an error or a step on the same view already holds it; then the ampersand takes the headline’s ink, as Rule 04.3 sets out.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-display"Inter Tight", Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-color-palette-pillar-red#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

When one half is red or heavier, the headline takes a side between a rule and its result. Equal halves leave the joining to the ampersand.

Specifications

  • work/build/assets/identity/ampersand/20261028_Amp-B-24px-Master.svg
  • work/build/assets/identity/ampersand/20261028_Amp-B-Display-Master.svg

Related chapters

  • 04 The Ampersand and the hinge
  • 02 Voice

For builders

Set the headline in Inter Tight ExtraBold and place ampersand B at the cap height in place of the font’s ampersand, from the master Rule 04.3 names for the size.

Rule 01.19 Join people through a rule or place they share, and rotate their order.

When a hinge headline joins two people or groups, join them through a rule or a place they share. Swap their order from one piece to the next, so neither always comes first.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The ampersand stands for common ground, and people stand on it through something they share. A fixed order would rank one group above the other.

Related chapters

  • 04 The Ampersand and the hinge
  • 02 Voice

For builders

Log the order of each pair of people, and swap it the next time a piece joins the same two groups.

Rule 01.20 Name parties, the left or the right in a hinge headline only to report sourced agreement.

Use “left”, “right” or a party’s name in a hinge headline only to report a point where the sides agree, such as a bill with sponsors from both parties. Join the two through what they agree on, as Rule 01.19 asks of every pair of people, and source the agreement in the deck.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A red ampersand between two sides would mark the sides themselves, against Rule 01.1. Reporting agreement is the one case where naming the sides helps a reader.

Related chapters

  • 04 The Ampersand and the hinge
  • 02 Voice

For builders

When a headline names the sides, link the deck’s source line to the vote, the sponsor list or the survey that shows the agreement.

Group 6 Labels, Act pieces and names

Tell a reader what kind of piece they are reading, and name each product for what it does.

Rule 01.21 Open every kicker with one content label.

Open the kicker, the short line above a headline, with one of the seven content labels in this rule’s specifications. At most one more part follows, after a middle dot: the series name if the piece belongs to a series, otherwise its topic, as in “Explainer · Local schools”. A newsletter issue carries no label in its header, and each story inside it carries its own.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-action-primary-fill-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The label tells a reader what kind of claim the piece makes before they read it, and whether we are reporting or arguing.

Specifications

Explainer
How a rule or a decision works
Tracker
Where a decision stands, dated “as of”
Analysis
What the evidence shows on a contested question
Report
A numbered study, with its method and its date
Guide
How to reach the office that decides, for a Connect piece
Act · How to take part
One step with its date and place; one label, with nothing after it
Our position
An argument for or against a named measure, in the Charcoal label (Rule 01.23)
--oa-color-action-primary-fill-on-newsprint
Never a kicker
A pillar name alone, and a chart’s “Finding” line, which sits above the chart’s title as its evidence line
Type
The label style, Inter 700 capitals at 13 px; the second part in the secondary text ink

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later
  • 08 The Signal Grid

For builders

Pick the label from the seven in this rule. If a piece fits none of them, ask the editor before it runs. Rule 08.8 sets the grid and icon that may lead a kicker.

Rule 01.22 In a process piece, name the step and leave the side to the reader.

An Act piece labeled “Act · How to take part” gives one step with its date and place, sets out what supporters and opponents have said at the same length, and takes no side. Its ask is the view’s one working red.

  • --oa-component-button-ask-keyline-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader of any view can use a process piece, because it tells them how to be heard and leaves what to say to them.

Specifications

Act · How to take part, the label alone
Ask
Pillar Red fill, White label at 19 px bold, Charcoal keyline on Newsprint

For builders

Build the ending from the hinge divider, the “What you can do” line and one ask button. Link the neutral tracker, never a campaign page.

Rule 01.23 Put a position piece’s label before the headline and its fairness kit before the ask.

A piece that asks readers to support or oppose a named measure opens its kicker with the label “Our position”, before the headline. Before the ask it carries the fairness kit, the eight parts in this rule’s specifications, among them the strongest case against the position, what we don’t know and who decided.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-action-primary-fill-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A reader who disagrees with us can still trust the rest of our coverage when each argument carries its label, its strongest opposing case and the names of the people who decided it.

Specifications

Label first
“Our position” opens the kicker, before the headline, and a shared card keeps it top left.
The strongest case against
The opposing case as its supporters would put it, sourced, at least a third of the argument’s length.
Grades kept
Every claim keeps its evidence grade, and its verb matches the grade.
Opponents by role
Name opponents by office or role, and cast no party as a villain.
What we don’t know
The open questions, named.
Process facts
Who decides, when and how, word for word as the neutral tracker gives them.
Disclosure
Who decided the position and when, any funder’s interest in the measure, and links to the bios of those who decided, above the ask.
Kept out of the record
Positions stay out of the atlas, the trackers and the data.

  • 18 Components and interaction Coming later

For builders

Use the position label component, never a plain kicker, and check the eight parts of the kit in this rule’s specifications before the piece goes to the editor.

Rule 01.24 Name each product for what it does, and keep the ampersand for Oath & Action.

Give each product a plain name that says what it does, signed by Oath & Action. The atlas is the only product named as a question, and no product name holds an ampersand. When we type a partner’s name in our own copy, its ampersand becomes “and”, and the partner’s logo stays as the partner draws it.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Every product carries one name, Oath & Action, so a reader who trusts the newsletter can trust the tracker it links to. A plain name tells them what they will get before they open it.

Related chapters

  • 03 Identity
  • 22 Newsletter and email Coming later

For builders

Name a new product as its subject plus its kind, such as “Child Care Rules Tracker”, and check the name against this rule and Rule 01.15 before it ships. A piece made with a partner goes to Dustin Cathcart, our founder and editor, or an editor he names, before it prints or posts, and the host’s name leads. Chapter 03 sets the partnership lockup.

Foundations · Chapter 02 of 28

02 Voice

Write the way you’d explain a rule to a neighbor, and quote the brand lines exactly.

Our tagline is “A country that answers to its people.” People can hold an office to account once they know which office decided. So we name who acts, in words you would use at a kitchen table, as in “A regulator or a board approves your rate.”

Our reader promise is “We explain how a decision is made and give you a practical way to take part.” A reader can take part only in a decision they can follow, which is why clarity comes first in our editorial commitment, “Clarity is our duty. Action is our promise.”

Rules in this chapter, by group

  1. 1 Sound like a person talking
    • 02.1 W01 Write it the way you would say it.
    • 02.2 W02 Name who acts.
    • 02.3 W03 Change the length of your sentences.
    • 02.4 W04 Join thoughts that belong together.
  2. 2 Put the point first and stop
    • 02.5 W05 Open with something the reader can use.
    • 02.6 W06 Give the point without a reveal.
    • 02.7 W07 Stop when the facts stop.
    • 02.8 W08 Close without a slogan.
  3. 3 Say what is so
    • 02.9 W09 Say what a thing is.
    • 02.10 W10 Drop the matched pair.
    • 02.11 W11 Skip the run of negatives.
    • 02.12 W12 List what the facts hold.
    • 02.13 W13 Give each sentence its own shape.
  4. 4 Cut the padding
    • 02.14 W14 Pull stacked nouns apart.
    • 02.15 W15 Use the verb inside the noun.
    • 02.16 W16 Drop the hedges and keep the grade.
    • 02.17 W17 Cut the intensifiers.
    • 02.18 W18 Use everyday verbs.
    • 02.19 W19 Let the facts carry the feeling.
    • 02.20 W20 Size each word to its evidence.
  5. 5 Marks and numbers
    • 02.21 W21 Leave out the em dash.
  6. 6 House rules for every page
    • 02.22 Follow the 12 house rules on every page.
  7. 7 Our lines and words
    • 02.23 Set each brand line in its own place, word for word.
    • 02.24 Close every piece on one next step, with its date.
    • 02.25 Publish the mechanism behind a mood.
    • 02.26 Use the words a reader would use, and spell series names exactly.

Group 1 Sound like a person talking

Write the sentence you would say across a kitchen table, with the actor up front and a rhythm that keeps changing.

Rule 02.1 W01 Write it the way you would say it.

Write the way you would explain something to a neighbor, in everyday words and full sentences. Read the draft aloud and rewrite any line you would not say.

Terms. Plain prose: everyday words in complete sentences, with nothing a listener would need to see on the page to follow.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Most readers meet us on a phone, between other things. A sentence they can follow by ear the first time is the one they can act on.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before
Our brand guide, fifth edition, the sample research brief in its Reports chapter

Related chapters

  • 01 Purpose

For builders

Read the draft aloud, or have a screen reader read it to you, and rewrite each line where you stumble or stop to decode.

Rule 02.2 W02 Name who acts.

Put the person or office that acts in front of the verb. When you find a passive verb, ask who does the action and name them.

Terms. Active voice: a sentence that names the actor first, as in “The council passed the budget.” Passive voice puts the thing acted on first and often hides the actor, as in “The budget was passed.”

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

People can hold an office to account only when they can name it. Putting the actor first gives them the name in the first breath.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before
Our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, the everyday answer to “Why is my electric bill going up?”

Related chapters

  • 01 Purpose
  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later

For builders

Search for “is”, “are”, “was” and “were” before a past participle, and for “by”, and ask who does the action.

Rule 02.3 W03 Change the length of your sentences.

Mix short sentences with long ones, and keep the mix hard to predict. A run of sentences the same size starts to sound like a metronome.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Speech rises and falls. When every sentence runs the same length, a listener starts to hear the beat over the words.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before
Our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, reform profile “Rules for drug-pricing middlemen (PBMs)”, how it would be carried out

For builders

Count the words in each sentence of a paragraph. If every count falls within a few words of the others, join two sentences or split one.

Rule 02.4 W04 Join thoughts that belong together.

Use the small words that show how thoughts connect, such as because, so, when and once. Save short sentences for the moments that need one.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Words such as because and once carry the logic a listener needs. Without them, the reader has to guess how one short sentence leads to the next.

Specifications

Group
1. Sound like a person talking
Before
Our brand guide, fifth edition, chapter 02 Voice, sample lines

For builders

Look for runs of short sentences with no joining word, and join the ones that depend on each other with because, so, when or once.

Group 2 Put the point first and stop

Open with what the reader came for, and end when the facts run out.

Rule 02.5 W05 Open with something the reader can use.

Make the first sentence give the reader a fact or a step. Cut lines that only announce what comes next, and stock phrases that lean on the words after them.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A reader decides in the first line whether a piece is worth their time, and a line that only announces what is coming gives them no reason to stay.

For builders

Delete the first sentence of a draft and read it again. If nothing is lost, leave it out.

Rule 02.6 W06 Give the point without a reveal.

Put the point where the reader meets it first. A colon or a teaser sentence that holds it back for effect only makes the reader wait.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A reveal makes the reader wait for a point we could have given at once, and holding it back sounds like a performance.

For builders

Search headlines and openers for colons and for “here’s”, “this is where” and “the answer”, and lead with what follows them.

Rule 02.7 W07 Stop when the facts stop.

End a paragraph on its last useful fact, and cut any line after it that only restates the point.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A closing line that restates the point tells the reader we doubt they followed, so we end on the last new fact and trust them with it.

Cover the last sentence of each paragraph. If the paragraph still holds every fact, delete the sentence.

Rule 02.8 W08 Close without a slogan.

End a piece or section on the last thing the reader needs, usually a step with its date. Where a sign-off line belongs, use the locked tagline.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

The last words of a piece are the ones a reader carries away. A dated step gives them something to do with what they read.

Group 3 Say what is so

State what is true in plain sentences, and leave out the shapes writers use for effect.

Rule 02.9 W09 Say what a thing is.

Tell the reader what something is. Leave out the turn that first says what it is not, and the phrases set against each other for effect.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A sentence that starts with what a thing is not makes the reader picture the wrong thing first and then undo it.

For builders

Search for “, not”, “not only” and “rather than”, and keep the half that says what to do.

Rule 02.10 W10 Drop the matched pair.

Write the relation between two things as a plain sentence. Two short halves set side by side sound like a slogan and leave the reader to supply the link.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Two matched halves sound like a slogan and leave the reader to supply the link between them, which one plain sentence can state.

For builders

Look for pairs of short sentences that repeat a word or a frame, and write the relation between them in one sentence.

Rule 02.11 W11 Skip the run of negatives.

When you rule several things out, put them in one list under one verb and give the reason.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A run of negatives sounds like a list of grievances. One verb and a reason tell the reader what to do and why.

Rule 02.12 W12 List what the facts hold.

Give a list as many items as the facts hold. When there are three, vary their shape so they do not fall into a chant.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Three items in a row sound finished, so writers reach for three when the facts hold two or four. A list sized to the facts sounds like advice.

Rule 02.13 W13 Give each sentence its own shape.

Build each sentence in a paragraph on its own frame. When several in a row open the same way, combine them or recast one.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

When sentences in a row open the same way, a listener hears the pattern and stops hearing the content.

Group 4 Cut the padding

Take out the words that add weight and no meaning.

Rule 02.14 W14 Pull stacked nouns apart.

When three or more nouns pile up, pull them apart with a preposition or a verb, so a listener can find the main noun.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A listener holds each noun in a stack until the last one says what the phrase is about. Pulling the stack apart puts the main noun first.

For builders

Search for three or more nouns in a row, and rewrite with a preposition or a verb between them.

Rule 02.15 W15 Use the verb inside the noun.

When a noun hides a verb, use the verb and name who does it.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A noun made from a verb hides who acts, and turning it back into the verb brings the actor back into the sentence.

Rule 02.16 W16 Drop the hedges and keep the grade.

State a claim at the strength its evidence holds. When the evidence grade calls for “may” or “can”, use that word once and cut the other softeners.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

One grade verb, taken from the atlas’s scale, tells a reader how far the evidence goes. A pile of softeners leaves them to guess.

Rule 02.17 W17 Cut the intensifiers.

Cut words that try to add force, such as genuinely, really, truly, actually, simply and just. If the sentence feels weak without one, give it a stronger fact.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A word added for force signals that the sentence is missing a fact, and the fact, once found, carries the force by itself.

Rule 02.18 W18 Use everyday verbs.

Pick the word you would say out loud. Write “use” for leverage, and “show” for underscore or reflect.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A resident at a council meeting says “use” and “show”, and copy in those words sounds like a neighbor talking.

Rule 02.19 W19 Let the facts carry the feeling.

Leave out exclamation points and cheering, and let the step itself carry the energy.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Excitement on the page asks the reader to feel something we have given them no reason for, and a clear step with its date gives them the reason.

Rule 02.20 W20 Size each word to its evidence.

Give an adjective or a label no more weight than its evidence carries, and when we praise our own work, label the praise as a design judgment.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A word that claims more than the evidence invites a reader to check it and find it wrong, and one wrong word costs the trust the rest of the page earned.

Group 5 Marks and numbers

Set dashes, dates, numbers and signs the same way on every page.

Rule 02.21 W21 Leave out the em dash.

Where you want an em dash, end the sentence, or join the parts with a comma and a word such as “and” or “because”.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

An em dash lets a writer skip the word that says how two thoughts connect, and a listener needs that word to follow.

Group 6 House rules for every page

Twelve rules hold on every page, from quoting the locked lines exactly to calling a contested policy by its neutral name, and H05 to H07 also belong to group 5.

Rule 02.22 Follow the 12 house rules on every page.

Every page follows the 12 house rules, from quoting the locked lines exactly to calling a contested policy by its neutral name. They apply to headings, labels, captions and chart keys as well as to sentences.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

These are details a reader relies on without noticing, such as a date written in words and a source line they can follow back to its table. Each one keeps a page easy to check and fair to every reader.

Group 7 Our lines and words

Quote each brand line in its own place, and write everything around it in the words a reader would use.

Rule 02.23 Set each brand line in its own place, word for word.

Each brand line has one job and a set of places where it appears, as the table of brand lines gives them. Quote it exactly there, and keep the founding line out of the tagline’s slot.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A line that appears in the same place every time becomes something a reader recognizes. Moving a line, or swapping one in, spends that recognition.

Copy brand lines from the table in this chapter, never retype them, and check them character for character before a piece ships.

Rule 02.24 Close every piece on one next step, with its date.

End every piece on the one step a reader is most likely to take, with its date and place and the way to take it. Link other ways to take part from the step’s page. In a newsletter, the step ends the last story, and the tagline follows it as the issue’s sign-off.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Four asks at the end of a piece leave a reader to choose, and most choose none. One dated step is easy to take before the date passes.

  • 01 Purpose
  • 12 Graphic devices and patterns Coming later
  • 22 Newsletter and email Coming later

For builders

Give the piece one ask button and put the other ways to take part on the page the button opens. In an email, the tagline after the last story is the sign-off.

Rule 02.25 Publish the mechanism behind a mood.

When a draft states a sweeping claim, a feeling, a slogan or a side, replace it with the mechanism behind it: the rule, the office that decides, the step a reader can take or the structure of the vote.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A mood asks the reader to agree with us, and the mechanism behind it gives them something to check and an office to call.

Related chapters

  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later
  • 01 Purpose

For builders

For each sentence of a draft, ask which rule, office, date or count it rests on. Where the answer is none, the sentence is a mood.

Rule 02.26 Use the words a reader would use, and spell series names exactly.

Write rule, decision, record, hearing and vote, the words a reader uses for public business. Leave out the words this rule lists, define each term of art at first use, and spell the six series names exactly.

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

Every word on the list to leave out has a plainer one that says more. Exact series names let a reader find a series again.

Related chapters

  • 08 The Signal Grid
  • 13 Evidence and sourcing Coming later

For builders

Search a draft for every word on the list to leave out, and check each series name against the list before a kicker ships.

Rule 02.27 Write a hinge headline as a rule, then what it produces.

A hinge headline joins two noun phrases with the ampersand. The first names a rule, and the second names what the rule produces in a reader’s life. A headline that joins two people or groups follows Rules 01.19 and 01.20, Rule 01.18 sets its color, and Rule 04.3 sets how it is drawn.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-display"Inter Tight", Arial, sans-serif

Why it works

Basis Editorial judgment

A reader meets the rule they could change beside the result they already feel, which is the hinge between a commitment and the action that keeps it.

Foundations · Chapter 03 of 28

03 Identity

Pick the lockup that fits the surface and size, and give it room on every side.

The wordmark is our name drawn as one piece of artwork: OATH and ACTION in heavy capitals, joined by ampersand B, the red ampersand we drew for Oath & Action. A lockup is a fixed arrangement of the wordmark with another part, such as the tagline or the lockmark, the 3 by 3 grid of nodes that chapter 08 explains.

Every mark here is a vector master drawn for a range of sizes. You place the master, color it with tokens and leave room around it. In this chapter x means the height of the wordmark’s capitals, and the pages show today’s wordmark width. The condensed width, which Dustin Cathcart is weighing, appears only in the wordmark width proofs after chapter 08.

In this chapter

  • Rule 03.1 Place the wordmark from its master file.
  • Rule 03.2 Choose the lockup by the space and the surface.
  • Rule 03.3 Keep one cap height of clear space on every side.
  • Rule 03.4 Keep every mark at or above its minimum size.
  • Rule 03.5 Set the marks in their colors on the four approved surfaces.
  • Rule 03.6 Use L3 for the masthead, and drop the lockmark when the bar gets narrow.
  • Rule 03.7 Use L8 as the one monogram, and retire the spaced “O & A”.
  • Rule 03.8 Join a partner with a hairline, and keep our ampersand inside our name.

Rule 03.1 Place the wordmark from its master file.

Use the master drawn for the height you need and set its color with tokens. Never type the name in a font, Inter Tight included, though the capitals were cut from it.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The masters set every gap between letters by eye and give the ampersand the same white on each side, 0.203x, so the name keeps one shape from a 16 px email footer to a printed banner. Ampersand B exists only as drawn artwork. A typed name takes the font’s ampersand and the font’s spacing, and a reader who meets two slightly different names starts to wonder which one is ours.

Rule 03.2 Choose the lockup by the space and the surface.

Eight lockups cover every use, and each has one job. Start from the width you have: L1 for most uses, L3 for the site and email masthead, L2 for square formats and posters, L8 where the full name will not fit. The sheet after this rule shows all eight at true size, and the specifications give each one’s minimum.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A fixed set means a reader meets the same arrangement in the same place, and a producer never has to invent one. Each lockup’s job comes from the space it fills, so the choice turns on two facts you can measure: the width you have and the surface under it.

Rule 03.3 Keep one cap height of clear space on every side.

Leave 1.0x of open space around the lockup’s outer edge, with its tagline and lockmark inside that edge. Text, rules, image edges and other logos all stay outside it. In a partnership lockup the hairline and the partner’s logo belong to the lockup, so the clear space runs around all three (Rule 03.8). Over a photograph, set the lockup on a solid Newsprint or Charcoal panel with the same space inside the panel.

Tokens

  • --oa-space-4002rem

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Open space lets the eye find the name before it reads anything else, and it keeps a headline or a partner’s logo from reading as part of our mark. A measure of one cap height grows with the mark, so the rule holds at every size.

Round the clear space up to the next step of the spacing scale, so a page built on the 8 px rhythm keeps it.

Rule 03.4 Keep every mark at or above its minimum size.

On screen, no identity mark draws its capitals under 14 px, and no tagline inside a lockup sets under 13 px. In print, no capitals under 3 mm and no tagline under 7 pt. Under a lockup’s minimum, switch to the lockup the table names.

Why it works

Basis Our measurements, October 2026

Each master was drawn and checked at its smallest size, where the wordmark keeps its six enclosed counters, the holes inside letters such as O and A, and the ampersand keeps its two. Our fifth edition scaled one drawing to every size, and at its own 120 px minimum a notch in the ampersand closed into a seventh enclosed shape.

Rule 03.5 Set the marks in their colors on the four approved surfaces.

Newsprint, White and Charcoal carry the wordmark with its red ampersand. On Prussian every mark goes White, ampersand and lever included, because red never sits on Prussian (Rule 05.3). One-color versions in Charcoal or White serve one-color print, embossing and watermarks.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-charcoal#DCD9D2
  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-charcoal#E63946
  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-prussian#FFFFFF

Why it works

Basis Design judgment, measured against WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 at rendered sizes; Rule 05.3 for red

Each surface has one ink that reads on it: Charcoal on Newsprint at 13.29:1, Newsprint on Charcoal at 13.29:1, White on Prussian at 13.28:1. Pillar Red measures 3.19:1 on Prussian, just over the 3:1 a graphic needs, but once drawn small it falls short: our fifth edition’s red ampersand measured 2.27:1 there at 16 px. Red on our dark blue also reads as a pair of party colors, which Rule 01.1 keeps off every page.

Rule 03.6 Use L3 for the masthead, and drop the lockmark when the bar gets narrow.

The masthead is the bar across the top of every page and email. From 48em wide, 768 px at the default text size, it sets L3: the wordmark at left and the lockmark at its right, 2.4 cap heights tall. Under 48em, it sets L1 from the 24 px master beside the menu button. Email takes L3 as an image.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The masthead is the one place every reader sees the mark, so it carries the fullest lockup the width allows. The lockmark needs about 34 px to show its nine nodes and its lever, and on a phone that room goes to the menu button.

Rule 03.7 Use L8 as the one monogram, and retire the spaced “O & A”.

L8 sets O and A with ampersand B between them, cut from the same masters as the wordmark. It serves small squares where the full name will not fit, from 48 px wide. The compact signature from our brand guide’s fourth edition, “O & A” typed with word spaces, retires, along with any other typed monogram.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Two monograms split what readers learn to recognize. L8 keeps the wordmark’s own white beside the ampersand, so it reads as the name in brief. Typed with spaces, the three characters read as separate letters, and the font’s ampersand replaces B.

Rule 03.8 Join a partner with a hairline, and keep our ampersand inside our name.

In a partnership lockup the host’s name leads: on a piece we host, L1 sits at left; on a piece the partner hosts, the partner’s logo sits at left and L1 follows. A 1 px vertical hairline stands between them with 0.6x of space on each side, and the partner’s logo stands no taller than our capitals. For a square, set L8 beside the partner’s logo the same way. Our ampersand stays inside the wordmark, and a second ampersand or a plus sign never joins the two names.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-border-hairline-on-newsprint#5D636D

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Dustin Cathcart’s ruling on partners, November 6, 2026

The ampersand is our hinge between an oath and the action that keeps it. Used to join two organizations, it turns our mark into a conjunction anyone can borrow, and the reader sees one organization with a long name. A hairline marks a partnership and gives each name its own field, and the host leads because a reader first wants to know who is holding the event.

Specifications

The host’s name leads, at left
Hairline

Foundations · Chapter 04 of 28

04 The Ampersand and the hinge

Use the ampersand once per composition to join a commitment to what it produces.

The ampersand is the hinge of the brand. It joins an oath, the commitment a person or an office makes, to the action that keeps it, and in our headlines it joins a rule to its result. Ampersand B is our own drawing: one pen path that crosses itself at the waist, with a beak at the top right and a tail that lands on the baseline.

This chapter covers B drawn alone and the four places the hinge appears: the hinge headline, the hinge divider, the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge. It ends with the tiles for avatars and the app icon, and the large crop for covers.

In this chapter

  • Rule 04.1 Draw the ampersand from B’s master for its size.
  • Rule 04.2 Give each composition one ampersand moment.
  • Rule 04.3 Join a rule to its result with a hinge headline, and give its ampersand the view’s working red.
  • Rule 04.4 Set a hinge divider between how a decision is made and what you can do about it.
  • Rule 04.5 Show the hinge diagram on its own, to explain the idea.
  • Rule 04.6 Use the hinge-circle badge only to close a piece, on a back cover or at events.
  • Rule 04.7 Put B on a Charcoal tile for avatars and the app icon.
  • Rule 04.8 Crop a large B off the bottom-right corner only.

Rule 04.1 Draw the ampersand from B’s master for its size.

B has three masters: the 16 px master for 16 to 23 px tall, the 24 px master for 24 to 47 px, and the display master from 48 px. Place the one whose range holds your height. A narrow drawing of B serves the condensed wordmark alone.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Our measurements, October 2026

B’s strokes swell and thin at 1.74 to 1, so the glyph keeps its color beside the heavy capitals, and its waist crossing sits on the center line that the hinge diagram draws through its nodes. The small masters sit on the pixel grid: at 16 px, 66 percent of B’s ink pixels are solid, where the glyph in our brand guide’s fifth edition reached 48 percent.

Specifications

Stroke contrast
1.74 to 1, thickest over thinnest
Weight
Thick strokes at 0.91 of the wordmark’s stem
Waist crossing
On the glyph’s vertical ink center
Overshoot
1.34 wordmark units above the cap line and below the baseline
Clear space, drawn alone
1.0x of B’s own cap height
Color
Signature red; White on Prussian
--oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint

Rule 04.2 Give each composition one ampersand moment.

A composition is one view: a screen, a card, a slide or a printed page. It carries one ampersand moment, a hinge headline, a freestanding B or a cropped B. The wordmark’s own ampersand and the hinge divider do not count.

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The ampersand carries the brand’s idea, and a reader takes in one hinge at a time. With two or three on a card, each says less and the eye has no place to land.

Specifications

Moments
A hinge headline, a freestanding B or a cropped B
Not counted
The wordmark’s ampersand and the hinge divider

  • 05 Color

For builders

When a template already holds a hinge headline, leave its ampersand slot out of every other layer.

Rule 04.3 Join a rule to its result with a hinge headline, and give its ampersand the view’s working red.

A hinge headline joins two noun phrases with B, as in “The zoning code & the rent.” B takes the view’s working red, the one red each view may spend, unless an error or a step the reader can take now already holds it. Then B takes the headline’s ink. Rule 02.27 sets how to write one, and Rules 01.18 to 01.20 set when to use one.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946
  • --oa-color-action-ask-fill-on-newsprint#E63946

Why it works

Basis Rule 05.3, the red rule

The headline names a mechanism in five or six words, and the red ampersand marks the joint. Rule 05.3 ranks an error first and the step a reader can take now second, so on an Act piece with a red button the step keeps the red.

Master
16 px master under 22 px capitals, 24 px master to 46 px, display above

Rule 04.4 Set a hinge divider between how a decision is made and what you can do about it.

The hinge divider centers B’s 24 px master on a 1 px line as wide as the text it divides, with 12 px of clear line on each side of B. Line and B take the surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. It is never red.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-hinge-divider-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-identity-hinge-divider-on-charcoal#DCD9D2
  • --oa-color-identity-hinge-divider-on-prussian#FFFFFF

Why it works

Basis Rule 05.3, the red rule; Design judgment

The divider marks the turn from how a decision is made to the step a reader can take, the same turn the ampersand makes in our name. In ink it stays quiet, and the view’s one working red stays free for the step itself.

Rule 04.5 Show the hinge diagram on its own, to explain the idea.

The hinge diagram draws OATH and ACTION on a line with four nodes, B in a ring between them, two solid arcs running clockwise, and UNDERSTAND and IMPACT beneath. Draw its lines solid, give it words alone, and keep it out of any view that holds the wordmark, the badge or a figure with a key. Where a page needs a break, use the divider.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint#E63946
  • --oa-color-graphic-subtle-on-newsprint#5D636D

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

The diagram teaches the brand’s idea in one picture: a promise becomes action, and the result shapes the next promise. Its arcs are solid because our systems atlas draws a hypothesis as a dotted line and a plausible link as a dashed one. It carries words alone, with no ID, sign, grade, delay or count, so no reader takes it for one of the atlas’s loops.

Specifications

Display master
From 533 px wide, labels at 13 px; 4.00 in in print
Compact master
From 245 px wide, no labels
Lines
Solid; 3.5 units, arcs 2.8 units on the display master
B
In the ring, 1.25 cap heights, signature red
Below 245 px
A hinge headline

Rule 04.6 Use the hinge-circle badge only to close a piece, on a back cover or at events.

The badge is B inside the hinge diagram’s ring, with no words. It ends an article or a report and marks event materials. Keep it off anything about a candidate or a ballot measure, where a seal-like mark could read as an endorsement. Keep it away from avatars, favicons and any view with the wordmark or the hinge diagram, and add no words or dates to it.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-identity-signature-on-charcoal#E63946

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A ring of words and a founding date turn a badge into a seal, and our fifth edition put the reason plainly: “Seals imply an authority we do not claim.” A wordless badge closes a piece the way a period closes a sentence.

Specifications

Masters
16 px from 16 to 23 px, 24 px from 24 to 47 px, display from 48 px
Print

Color
Signature red, ring and B alike; White on Prussian
--oa-color-identity-signature-on-newsprint
Print finishes
A blind emboss on uncoated stock, matte red foil on Charcoal, or one color; chapter 25 sets the details

Rule 04.7 Put B on a Charcoal tile for avatars and the app icon.

Social avatars and the app icon show B alone on a Charcoal tile, a circle for avatars and a square for the app icon. The platform prints the account name beside an avatar, so the mark can be the ampersand alone. Favicons use B’s 16 px master with no tile.

Tokens

  • --oa-component-avatar-tile#121212
  • --oa-component-avatar-accent#E63946
  • --oa-component-app-icon-tile#121212

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11; Design judgment for the feed sizes

A feed often draws an avatar at 32 to 48 px. B’s 24 px master still reads there, where any lettered mark would set its capitals under the 14 px floor. Charcoal is the default tile because it holds Pillar Red at 4.49:1, the strongest red of any approved surface, and stays visible on light and dark app themes.

Rule 04.8 Crop a large B off the bottom-right corner only.

On a cover or a section opener, a large B may run off the bottom-right corner with up to 40 percent of the glyph outside the frame. It takes the surface’s ink, stays clear of the text, and never enters the top-left corner where reading starts.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Rule 05.3

Readers start at the top left, so a crop there sits in the way of the title. At the bottom right it frames the page and points to the turn. Rule 05.3 gives red no job for a crop, so it takes the surface’s ink, as the divider does.

Specifications

/* tokens.css is the full source of these values: download it from this page and link it before your own styles.
   This block copies, as tokens.css holds them, the custom properties chapter 04 names, every property they
   depend on and the four surface classes, so it also works on its own. Set a page's ground with a surface
   class, as in <body class="oa-surface-newsprint">, and set type with font: var(--oa-type-body). */

Foundations · Chapter 05 of 28

05 Color

Choose a surface first, then the text and graphic colors that pass on it.

Oath & Action works in seven colors, and each one has a job. Newsprint, a warm off-white, is the page most of our work sits on, and Charcoal carries the words. Pillar Red marks the one thing a reader should see first in each view, meaning each screen, card, slide or printed page. The other four do narrower work: Prussian, our dark blue, holds panels of dates and figures, Stone draws hairlines, Verdigris, a muted green, shows success and focus, and White serves specimens and email.

Every pair in this chapter carries a contrast ratio, a measure of how far apart two colors sit in lightness. It runs from 1 to 1 for the same color up to 21 to 1 for black on white, by the formula in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). We measured each ratio on the token values, the exact colors our code names. Pick the surface first, and the tables tell you which text and marks can sit on it.

In this chapter

  • Rule 05.1 Cover most of every view in Newsprint.
  • Rule 05.2 Set text only on color pairs that pass.
  • Rule 05.3 Give each view one working red.
  • Rule 05.4 Show every state with a word or a shape as well as a color.
  • Rule 05.5 Keep marks that carry meaning at 3 to 1, and give red on Newsprint a Charcoal keyline.
  • Rule 05.6 Give each tint one named job, and keep tints off identity marks.
  • Rule 05.7 Set charts and the atlas on Newsprint, in the chart palette.

Rule 05.1 Cover most of every view in Newsprint.

Newsprint covers 60 to 85 percent of every view. A dark panel in Charcoal or Prussian marks a turn in the reading, so a section holds one at most, and Pillar Red stays within 5 percent. Across a body of work, the seven colors keep the shares in the palette sheet below this rule.

  • --oa-color-palette-stone#5D636D
  • --oa-color-palette-verdigris#4A7C74
  • --oa-color-palette-white#FFFFFF

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

A warm, light page keeps long reading calm, and readers come to know Newsprint as ours before they read a word. A dark panel works as a signal only while it stays rare. Each one tells the reader the section has turned, for example from an explanation to the dates that follow from it.

Set a page’s ground with its surface class, such as .oa-surface-newsprint. The class points the short names, such as --oa-color-text-primary, at that surface’s tokens, so a panel changes surface with one class.

Rule 05.2 Set text only on color pairs that pass.

Text under 24 px, or under 18.66 px in bold, needs a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 against its surface, and larger text needs 3 to 1. Take the primary and secondary text tokens for the surface. For any other pair, read its measured ratio in the tables below before you use it.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-white#121212
  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-charcoal#DCD9D2
  • --oa-color-text-primary-on-prussian#FFFFFF
  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-newsprint#4E535B

  • --oa-color-text-secondary-on-prussian#A3A19C

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) sets 4.5 to 1 for text and 3 to 1 for large text, which it defines as 18 point, or 14 point bold: 24 px and 18.66 px on screen. Readers with low vision need that margin, and so does anyone reading a phone in sunlight.

Stone, the secondary text color in our fifth edition, measures 4.29 to 1 on Newsprint. Secondary text on light surfaces now takes Deep Stone, Stone mixed 18 percent toward Charcoal, at 5.49 to 1. On dark surfaces it takes Dim Newsprint, Newsprint mixed 25 percent toward Charcoal, at 7.26 to 1 on Charcoal and 5.14 on Prussian.

For builders

Choose the surface, then the role: secondary text on Prussian is --oa-color-text-secondary-on-prussian. Inside a surface class, --oa-color-text-secondary resolves to the same value. A pair with no token is a pair we have not measured, so add a token under Rule 05.6 before you use it.

Rule 05.3 Give each view one working red.

The wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon’s red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red, and that red counts as signature red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline’s ampersand uses the view’s working red. The hinge divider’s ampersand takes its surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian.

  • --oa-component-button-ask-keyline-on-newsprint#121212
  • --oa-color-identity-hinge-divider-on-newsprint#121212

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

One red tells the eye where to go first. The order settles which mark gets it when two compete: a reader has to fix an error before taking a step, and a step a reader can take matters more than a point we want to make. Signature red is part of the marks themselves, so it never competes with the working red.

Red never sits on Prussian, where it measures 3.19 to 1 and reads as a party pair of red and blue. On Newsprint it measures 2.96 to 1, so a working red mark there takes a keyline, a 1 px Charcoal edge drawn inside the mark (Rule 05.5).

Count the reds before you ship a view. Mark each red element with data-red: signature for the marks, working with data-red-job for the one job. The shared check fails a view with two working jobs or any red over Prussian. When an error appears, swap the ask to --oa-component-button-primary-fill-on-newsprint.

Rule 05.4 Show every state with a word or a shape as well as a color.

Each interface state, from hover to error, changes its text or its shape along with its color. A disabled control stays readable and says what will make it available. State colors are their own set, kept apart from identity color and from the chart palettes in chapter 14.

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 and 1.4.11

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color asks that a state show something besides color, and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast asks 3 to 1 for the edges and focus rings that show one. Pillar Red and Verdigris measure 1.14 to 1 against each other, so a red error and a Verdigris success look alike to many readers unless a word and a glyph differ too.

For builders

Change two things in every state: the color and either the words or the shape. Use aria-disabled="true" so a disabled control keeps its focus and its reason line can be read. Never fade a control with opacity; take the state token instead.

Rule 05.5 Keep marks that carry meaning at 3 to 1, and give red on Newsprint a Charcoal keyline.

An icon, a chart mark, a control’s edge or a focus ring needs a ratio of 3 to 1 against its surface. Pillar Red measures 2.96 to 1 on Newsprint, so a red mark that carries meaning there takes a 1 px Charcoal keyline. Stone passes for marks on light surfaces, and a hairline that carries no meaning may sit lower.

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast asks 3 to 1 for the parts of a graphic a reader needs and for the edges of controls. The keyline gives a red mark an edge the eye can find, at 13.29 to 1, and the fill keeps its red. Stone context bars measure 4.29 to 1, so they pass without help.

For builders

Draw the keyline inside the shape, with box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px in HTML or a 1 px stroke on an inner path in SVG, so the mark keeps its size. On White and Charcoal, where red measures 4.17 and 4.49 to 1, a red mark needs no keyline.

Rule 05.6 Give each tint one named job, and keep tints off identity marks.

A tint is one palette color mixed toward Newsprint or Charcoal by a recorded amount, for one job. It enters only as a token, with its measured ratio. The wordmark, the ampersand, the lockmark and the pillar marks stay in solid palette colors, and no color on a page comes from lowering opacity.

Tokens

  • --oa-color-derived-deep-stone#4E535B
  • --oa-color-derived-dim-newsprint#A3A19C
  • --oa-color-derived-error-band#E1C9C1
  • --oa-color-tint-stone-n70#B4B4B3
  • --oa-color-tint-prussian-n62#8E94A4
  • --oa-color-tint-verdigris-n55#9AAEA6

Why it works

Basis Design judgment

Our fifth edition said “There are no tints.” Charts, error messages and selected rows need lighter and darker steps that no palette color supplies, so Edition 06 allows a tint that meets five conditions: a measured need, a recorded mix, one job, a passing ratio on every surface it serves and a registered token.

We mix in OKLab, a color space where equal steps look equal, which keeps a tint’s hue steady as it lightens. Opacity gives up that control. Charcoal at 40 percent on Newsprint measures 2.48 to 1, where the Deep Stone token measures 5.49.

For builders

Write a new tint as a recipe in the token source, such as mix('stone', 'newsprint', 0.70), and keep hex values out of pages. The generator computes the hex and every ratio, and the rule test fails a tint with no registered need. In CSS the same mix is color-mix(in oklab, var(--oa-color-palette-stone), var(--oa-color-palette-newsprint) 70%).

Rule 05.7 Set charts and the atlas on Newsprint, in the chart palette.

Newsprint is the page color for charts and the atlas. The series a title names takes Charcoal, and every other series takes Stone. When the title names one point, such as a single bar, that point takes the view’s working red with a Charcoal keyline, as in Rule 05.5. Values that rise and fall from a midpoint take the diverging scale, which runs from Prussian through a pale middle to Verdigris, with an arrow or a printed sign for the direction. Every party takes one neutral ink, with its name printed on the mark.

Tokens

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; Rules 01.1 and 01.3

Neither end of the diverging scale belongs to a party, so a reader sees a rise or a fall before any side. A scale from red to blue reads as a party split in the United States, and Rule 01.3 keeps it out of our charts. Both ends of our scale print as dark grays, so the arrow carries the direction for any reader who cannot tell the hues apart. On Newsprint, a chart shared on its own still reads as ours.

Foundations · Chapter 06 of 28

06 Type

Set every word at a readable size with the three faces and the type scale.

Three typefaces carry every word we publish: Inter Tight for headlines and big figures, Inter for reading and the interface, and Lora Italic for the words we quote. Each has a single job, so a reader can tell a headline from a quotation before reading either.

We set sizes in rem, a unit tied to the reader’s own text setting, which is 16 px unless they change it. A reader who enlarges text gets larger type everywhere, and no text on screen sets below 13 px.

In this chapter

  • Rule 06.1 Keep each typeface to its one job.
  • Rule 06.2 Take every size from the type scale.
  • Rule 06.3 Set no text on screen below 13 px.
  • Rule 06.4 Tighten tracking only as headings grow.
  • Rule 06.5 Line up figures in tables, and give negatives the true minus sign.
  • Rule 06.6 Balance a heading’s lines, and keep two words or more on its last line.
  • Rule 06.7 Hang opening quotation marks outside the text edge.
  • Rule 06.8 Set body text at 60 to 75 characters a line.
  • Rule 06.9 Set email type in the system font stack.
  • Rule 06.10 Load the three faces, and let no other face stand in.

Rule 06.1 Keep each typeface to its one job.

Inter Tight 800 sets titles, headings and big figures. Inter sets body text, the interface, labels, captions, tables and chart text, at 400, 600 and 700. Lora Italic sets only quoted words, such as a pull quote or a quote card, at 400, or at 500 on a quote card.

Tokens

  • --oa-font-family-display"Inter Tight", Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-readingInter, Arial, sans-serif
  • --oa-font-family-quoteLora, Georgia, serif
  • --oa-font-weight-extrabold800
  • --oa-font-weight-regular400
  • --oa-font-weight-semibold600
  • --oa-font-weight-bold700
  • --oa-font-weight-medium500

Why it works

Basis Our locked identity rules; design judgment

One face for each job lets a reader tell a headline from a quotation at a glance. The wordmark is drawn from Inter Tight 800, so our headings share its voice, and the page still reads as ours with the logo covered. Charts follow the same split: Inter Tight for titles, Inter for labels and numbers, and Lora Italic only for quoted words.

Specifications

Display
Inter Tight 800; fallback Arial, sans-serif
--oa-font-family-display
Reading and interface
Inter 400, 600 and 700; fallback Arial, sans-serif
--oa-font-family-reading
Quotation
Lora Italic 400, and 500 on quote cards; fallback Georgia, serif
--oa-font-family-quote
Source
Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License

Load all three with one link: https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@400;600;700&family=Inter+Tight:wght@800&family=Lora:ital,wght@1,400;1,500&display=swap. Then set faces only through --oa-font-family-display, --oa-font-family-reading and --oa-font-family-quote.

Rule 06.2 Take every size from the type scale.

Set text in the fourteen styles of the scale, with no sizes between them. On a web page, display styles grow with the window from 390 to 1440 px wide, and every size is in rem so it follows the reader’s text setting. A fixed artboard, such as a card, an email or a social image, takes fixed sizes from the same scale: up to 600 px wide, each style’s phone floor, and from 1,200 px wide, its desktop ceiling. Print pieces set type in points.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-titleInter Tight 800, 56 to 110 px, line height 0.95, tracking −3%
  • --oa-type-sectionInter Tight 800, 44 to 80 px, line height 1.03, tracking −2.5%
  • --oa-type-h3Inter Tight 800, 26 to 32 px, line height 1.08, tracking −1%
  • --oa-type-h4Inter Tight 800, 20 to 24 px, line height 1.15, tracking −0.5%
  • --oa-type-quoteLora 400, 24 to 32 px, line height 1.3, tracking −2%
  • --oa-type-introInter 400, 19 to 22 px, line height 1.5
  • --oa-type-bodyInter 400, 17 px, line height 1.6
  • --oa-type-body-smallInter 400, 15 px, line height 1.6
  • --oa-type-uiInter 600, 15 px, line height 1.4
  • --oa-type-captionInter 400, 14 px, line height 1.5
  • --oa-type-labelInter 700, 13 px, line height 1.4, tracking +6%
  • --oa-type-data-labelInter 600, 13 px, line height 1.3
  • --oa-type-figureInter Tight 800, 48 to 104 px, line height 1, tracking −3%
  • --oa-type-askInter 700, 19 px, line height 1.2

Why it works

Basis WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4; design judgment

WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text asks that text grow to 200 percent with nothing lost. A size in rem grows with the reader’s text setting, which a size fixed in px ignores. Our fifth edition set every size in px, and when our audit doubled its root text size, no text on the page grew.

A card or an email has one width, so the window cannot pick its sizes. Taking them from the scale’s two ends keeps a 480 px card and a 1,200 px social image in the same family as the page around them.

16 px, the browser default; every size is a multiple in rem

--oa-type-body

For builders

Set a style with its shorthand and its parts: font: var(--oa-type-body) carries face, weight, size and line height, and letter-spacing, text-transform and font-variant-numeric each have their own property, such as --oa-type-label-letter-spacing. On a fixed artboard, override only the size, as in font-size: 1.625rem for an H3 on a 480 px card. Never write a font size in px.

Rule 06.3 Set no text on screen below 13 px.

The smallest text on screen is 13 px, or 0.8125 rem: labels, tags and data labels. A label in capitals at 13 px takes Inter 700 with 6 percent tracking. A specimen that shows a mark or a minimum size at true size is a graphic, and its caption says so.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-labelInter 700, 13 px, line height 1.4, tracking +6%
  • --oa-type-data-labelInter 600, 13 px, line height 1.3
  • --oa-type-captionInter 400, 14 px, line height 1.5

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; our measurements of the fifth edition, October 2026

Our fifth edition set its labels at 10 to 12 px. Our census of its text, which measured 2,346 text elements rendered at 1440 px and left out text inside SVG drawings, counted 833 under 13 px. A floor with no screen exceptions keeps kickers, tags and navigation readable without zoom. At 13 px, capitals need less tracking than they did at 10 px, so 6 percent keeps them open without pulling a word apart.

--oa-type-label

--oa-type-data-label
Caption
Inter 400, 14 px, line height 1.5
--oa-type-caption

The shared check fails any text under 12.95 px, with SVG text measured at its rendered scale. A chart drawn in SVG has to keep its labels at 13 px on a phone, so draw a phone version rather than shrinking the desktop one.

Rule 06.4 Tighten tracking only as headings grow.

Tracking is the space added to or taken from every pair of letters. Display styles take negative tracking that eases as the size drops: −3 percent for titles, −2.5 percent for sections, −1 percent for H3 and −0.5 percent for H4. Big figures, which are digits, take −3 percent, and quotes in Lora Italic −2 percent. Reading styles keep the font’s own spacing, and labels in capitals open to +6 percent.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-titleInter Tight 800, 56 to 110 px, line height 0.95, tracking −3%
  • --oa-type-sectionInter Tight 800, 44 to 80 px, line height 1.03, tracking −2.5%
  • --oa-type-h3Inter Tight 800, 26 to 32 px, line height 1.08, tracking −1%
  • --oa-type-h4Inter Tight 800, 20 to 24 px, line height 1.15, tracking −0.5%
  • --oa-type-figureInter Tight 800, 48 to 104 px, line height 1, tracking −3%
  • --oa-type-labelInter 700, 13 px, line height 1.4, tracking +6%

Why it works

Basis Our measurements, November 2026; design judgment

At display sizes the font’s own spacing leaves gaps a reader sees, and a little negative tracking closes them. Pulled too far, the letters touch. Our fifth edition used −4.5 percent at every heading size from 24 to 110 px, and at the cover’s 110 px that makes 7 of our tagline’s 24 letter pairs touch. At the title’s −3 percent, two do.

Across the 23 rule titles in chapters 05 to 07, set at the H3 size of 32 px, 107 of 738 letter pairs touch at −3 percent, the value an early draft of this guide used, and 32 at −1 percent.

Tracking lives in each style’s letter-spacing property, in em, so it scales with the size: letter-spacing: var(--oa-type-h3-letter-spacing). Leave body text at the font’s own spacing.

Rule 06.5 Line up figures in tables, and give negatives the true minus sign.

Tables, trackers and chart labels set tabular figures, which give every digit the same width so a column lines up. A negative number takes the minus sign (−, U+2212), which matches the plus sign’s width, and the numbers in one column carry the same number of decimals.

Tokens

  • --oa-type-data-labelInter 600, 13 px, line height 1.3
  • --oa-type-figureInter Tight 800, 48 to 104 px, line height 1, tracking −3%
  • --oa-type-body-smallInter 400, 15 px, line height 1.6

Why it works

Basis Design judgment; chapter 02, house rule H07

A reader compares a column by its right edge, and proportional figures move that edge digit by digit. The hyphen is shorter than the minus and sits lower, so a hyphen before 245 can read as a dash. Chapter 02’s house rule H07 asks for the true minus in prose as well.

Specifications

Figures in tables and charts
Tabular, font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums
--oa-type-data-label
Big figures
Inter Tight 800, tabular
--oa-type-figure
Minus sign
− (U+2212); plus sign + (U+002B) where a sign is printed
Ligatures
Common on, discretionary off
